text: Merge word1 and word2 by alternating letters, starting with word1. If one is longer, append its remaining letters at the end.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Strictly alternate, one from word1, then one from word2, and when the shorter runs out, the rest of the longer is tacked on as-is? So a b plus p q r s gives a p b q r s?
Okay. This is a parallel two-pointer merge: a cursor in each string, advancing together.

Two ways to structure it. This problem reminds me of the merge step of merge sort: one cursor per sequence, but with a fixed alternation instead of a comparison. So I can loop while both have characters, taking one from each, then append whatever remains of the longer one. Or a single loop up to the max of m and n, guarded by i less than m and i less than n, which folds the leftover in automatically. Both are linear. I'll show the explicit one.

Here's the plan. One: while both cursors are in range, append word1 of l, then word2 of r, and move both. Two: if word1 has leftovers, append them. Three: if word2 has leftovers, append them. One thing worth flagging: after the main loop, at most one side has leftovers, since the loop stops as soon as either runs out. So the two tail appends are mutually exclusive. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Let me write it. The main loop takes word1 of l, then word2 of r, while both have characters. Then each leftover tail goes on in one piece with substr. Those two while loops end in a break, so they really act as ifs and run at most once. One detail worth flagging: res equals res plus builds a fresh string every step, copying the whole result, so the main loop is quadratic in the worst case. Plus-equals, or reserve and push back, keeps it linear. With both lengths at most a hundred, it's harmless here.

Let's dry-run a b c plus p q r s, expected a p b q c r s. The row that matters is when l reaches three: word1 is used up, so the loop stops. Word1 has no tail, but r is three, less than four, so word2's tail, s, is appended. That matches. Corner cases: equal length gives pure alternation, no tail. A b c d plus p q gives a p b q c d, from word1's tail. Single characters a and b give a b.

Time is linear in m plus n once appends are in place, since each character is placed exactly once. As written, the res equals res plus copy makes the main loop quadratic, which doesn't matter at a hundred characters. Space is m plus n for the output, plus two indices. One more thing: this is the parallel-cursor flavor of two pointers, distinct from the converging kind used for reversing or palindromes. Swap the fixed alternation for a comparison and it becomes merging two sorted arrays. Make one pointer advance only on a match and it's subsequence checking.

Nicely done. Three things stood out: framing it as a parallel-cursor merge, noticing the two tails are mutually exclusive, and catching that res equals res plus copies the string on every step. Good work.
